outline.chapter_title: Procedural Posture and Scope of Review
outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of the case, detailing the petitioners' journey from Colombia to the U.S. immigration system. It clarifies the specific legal claims remaining on appeal, distinguishes between abandoned and active arguments, and defines the highly deferential 'substantial evidence' standard that governs the Tenth Circuit's review of factual findings by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA).
subtopics: Factual Summary: The Jimenez Family's Political Activity and Conflict with Narco-Traffickers
Procedural History: From Notice to Appear to BIA Affirmance
Scope of Appeal: Limiting Issues to Asylum and Withholding of Removal
Standard of Review: Understanding the 'Substantial Evidence' Test and Administrative Record Constraints

outline.chapter_title: Defining Persecution: The Threshold of Harm
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the first element required for asylum eligibility: whether the petitioner suffered 'past persecution.' It explores the circuit's definition of persecution, emphasizing that threats and psychological distress alone are typically insufficient without accompanying physical harm or severe restrictions on liberty. The section dissects why the cumulative effect of the threats against the Jimenez family failed to meet this statutory threshold.
subtopics: Legal Definition of Persecution vs. Harassment or Discrimination
The Cumulative Effect Doctrine: Aggregating Incidents to Meet the Standard
Insufficiency of Threats Alone: Precedent on Verbal Warnings Without Physical Injury
Psychological and Emotional Harm: Why Fear and Stress Do Not Constitute Persecution in This Context

outline.chapter_title: The Nexus Requirement: Political Opinion vs. Personal Motive
outline.description: This chapter addresses the causal link ('nexus') required between the harm suffered and a statutorily protected ground. It focuses on the distinction between persecution based on 'political opinion' versus harm driven by personal vendettas or criminal enterprise interests. The analysis details how the court determined that the petitioners' political activism was merely tangential to the primary motive: protecting illegal revenue streams related to a property dispute.
subtopics: Statutory Protected Grounds: Focus on Political Opinion
The 'One Central Reason' Standard in Mixed-Motive Cases
Distinguishing Political Persecution from Criminal Retaliation
Application to Facts: How Property Disputes and Narco-Trafficking Interests Superseded Political Motives

outline.description: Even if past persecution were established, an applicant must demonstrate a well-founded fear of future persecution by showing state inability or unwillingness to protect them, or that internal relocation is unsafe. This chapter examines the evidentiary burden placed on applicants to report threats to authorities and explain why isolated negative interactions with police do not prove systemic government failure. It further explains the logic behind finding safe internal relocation feasible when threats are localized.
subtopics: State Ability and Willingness: The Duty to Report and Opportunity for Government Response
Systemic Failure vs. Individual Officer Apathy: Evaluating Evidence of Corruption
Rebutting Presumptions: The Feasibility and Reasonableness of Internal Relocation
Localized Threats: Why Moving Within Colombia Was Deemed a Viable Alternative
